title: Sequences
ks3: Algebra: sequences, term-to-term rules and the nth term
intro: Spot the pattern and keep it going. Practise term-to-term rules, special sequences, growing patterns and the nth term.
description: Free KS3 Maths sequences questions with answers: next terms, term-to-term rules, square and triangular numbers, Fibonacci, patterns and the nth term. Marked instantly, for Year 7, 8 and 9 (ages 9 to 14).

questions.q: What is the next number? 4, 9, 14, 19, …
questions.hint: How much does it go up by each time?
questions.explain: It goes up by 5 each time: 19 + 5 = 24.

questions.q: What is the next number? 50, 44, 38, 32, …
questions.hint: It goes down by the same amount each time.
questions.explain: It goes down by 6 each time: 32 − 6 = 26.

questions.q: What is the term-to-term rule for 3, 6, 12, 24, …?
questions.hint: The gaps are 3, 6, 12, so it is not adding the same number.
questions.explain: Each term is double the one before: 3 × 2 = 6, 6 × 2 = 12, 12 × 2 = 24.

questions.q: A sequence starts at 7 and the rule is "add 5". What is the 4th term?
questions.hint: Write out the terms: 7, 12, …
questions.explain: The terms are 7, 12, 17, 22. The 4th term is 22.

questions.q: What is the 6th term of 2, 6, 18, 54, …?
questions.hint: Each term is multiplied by the same number.
questions.explain: The rule is "multiply by 3": 54 × 3 = 162 (5th term) and 162 × 3 = 486 (6th term).

questions.q: What is the missing number? 7, 11, ?, 19, 23
questions.hint: Find the gap between the numbers you know.
questions.explain: It goes up by 4 each time: 11 + 4 = 15, and 15 + 4 = 19. ✓

questions.q: What is the next number? −8, −5, −2, 1, …
questions.hint: How much does it go up by each time? Count across zero carefully.
questions.explain: It goes up by 3 each time: −8, −5, −2, 1, so the next is 1 + 3 = 4.

questions.q: It is 6 °C at 6 pm, and the temperature falls by 3 °C every hour. What is the temperature at 10 pm?
questions.hint: Write the temperature for each hour: 6 pm 6 °C, 7 pm 3 °C, …
questions.explain: 6, 3, 0, −3, −6. So at 10 pm it is −6 °C (4 hours of falling 3 °C is 12 °C, and 6 − 12 = −6).

questions.q: What is the 8th term of 64, 32, 16, 8, …?
questions.hint: Each term is half of the one before. Keep going past 1.
questions.explain: Halve each time: 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, 0.5. The 8th term is 0.5 (or {1/2}).

questions.q: What is the next number? 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, …
questions.explain: These are the square numbers. The next is 6 × 6 = 36.

questions.q: What is the next number? 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, …
questions.hint: The gaps are 2, 3, 4, 5, …
questions.explain: These are the triangle numbers. The gaps grow by 1, so the next gap is 6: 15 + 6 = 21.

questions.q: What is the next number? 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, …
questions.hint: Look at the two numbers before each term.
questions.explain: Each term is the sum of the two before it (the Fibonacci sequence): 5 + 8 = 13.

questions.q: Which of these is a square number?
questions.hint: A square number is a number times itself, like 3 × 3 = 9.
questions.explain: 7 × 7 = 49, so 49 is a square number. 24, 18 and 50 are not: no whole number times itself gives them.

questions.q: What is the next number? 1, 8, 27, 64, …
questions.explain: These are the cube numbers. The next is 5 × 5 × 5 = 125.

questions.q: Look at the pattern. How many squares will Pattern 4 have?
questions.hint: How many squares are added each time?
questions.explain: Each pattern adds 2 squares: 3, 5, 7, so Pattern 4 has 9.

questions.q: Look at the pattern. How many squares will Pattern 10 have?
questions.hint: Pattern 1 has 3 squares and each new pattern adds 2. How many 2s are added to get to Pattern 10?
questions.explain: From Pattern 1 to Pattern 10 you add 2 nine times: 3 + 9 × 2 = 21. Or use the rule 2n + 1: 2 × 10 + 1 = 21.

questions.q: Look at the pattern. Which rule gives the number of squares in Pattern n?
questions.hint: It goes up by 2 each time, so the rule starts with 2n. Then check Pattern 1.
questions.explain: Going up by 2 means 2n. For Pattern 1, 2 × 1 = 2, but there are 3 squares, so add 1: 2n + 1. Check Pattern 3: 2 × 3 + 1 = 7. ✓

questions.q: Look at the pattern. How many squares will Pattern 4 have?
questions.hint: How many squares are added each time?
questions.explain: Each pattern adds 3 squares: 4, 7, 10, so Pattern 4 has 10 + 3 = 13.

questions.q: Look at the pattern. Which pattern number has 31 squares?
questions.hint: The rule is 3n + 1. Solve 3n + 1 = 31.
questions.explain: It goes up by 3 and Pattern 1 has 4, so the rule is 3n + 1. Then 3n + 1 = 31 → 3n = 30 → n = 10. Pattern 10 has 31 squares.

questions.q: The nth term of a sequence is 3n + 1. What is the 10th term?
questions.hint: Put n = 10 into 3n + 1.

questions.q: The nth term of a sequence is 5n − 2. What is the 1st term?
questions.hint: Put n = 1.

questions.q: What is the nth term of 5, 8, 11, 14, …?
questions.hint: It goes up by 3, so start with 3n. What do you add to 3 to get the first term, 5?
questions.explain: Going up by 3 means 3n. When n = 1, 3n = 3, and the first term is 5, so add 2: 3n + 2. Check: 3 × 4 + 2 = 14. ✓

questions.q: What is the nth term of 10, 8, 6, 4, …?
questions.hint: It goes down by 2, so it has −2n in it.
questions.explain: Going down by 2 means −2n. When n = 1, −2n = −2, and the first term is 10, so add 12: 12 − 2n. Check: 12 − 2 × 4 = 4. ✓

questions.q: Is 50 a term of the sequence with nth term 4n + 1?
questions.hint: Try solving 4n + 1 = 50. Does n come out as a whole number?
questions.explain: 4n + 1 = 50 gives 4n = 49 and n = 12.25, which is not a whole number, so 50 is not in the sequence. (Another way: 4n + 1 is always odd, and 50 is even.)

questions.q: The nth term of a sequence is 2n + 5. What is the 3rd term?
questions.hint: Put n = 3 into 2n + 5.

questions.q: What is the nth term of 4, 8, 12, 16, …?
questions.hint: These are the 4 times table.
questions.explain: It goes up by 4, so start with 4n. When n = 1, 4n = 4, which is already the first term, so the nth term is just 4n.

questions.q: The nth term of a sequence is n² + 1. What is the 5th term?
questions.hint: n² means n × n. Square first, then add 1.

questions.q: What is the nth term of 7, 12, 17, 22, …?
questions.hint: It goes up by 5, so start with 5n. What do you add to 5 to get the first term, 7?
questions.explain: Going up by 5 means 5n. When n = 1, 5n = 5, and the first term is 7, so add 2: 5n + 2. Check: 5 × 4 + 2 = 22. ✓
